=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Executive view

The Seller package materially shifts known and unknown risk to Wattlebridge despite the agreed debt-free/cash-free basis. The most important departures are:

1. **Riverlark debt and security are not cleared at Completion.**
2. **Bluefen consent is not yet obtained**, despite representing about 30% of revenue.
3. **At least AUD 420,000 of transaction bonuses and associated on-costs are omitted from funds flow.**
4. **Ironquay IP ownership remains conditional on an unpaid AUD 180,000 fee.**
5. **The privacy/export incident remains insufficiently investigated.**
6. **The liability regime would apply a low cap, short limitation period and exclusive remedy to virtually every claim, including title, tax, indemnities and potentially misconduct.**
7. **The sweeping data-room disclosure and constructive buyer-knowledge provisions could eliminate warranty protection without anything having been fairly disclosed.**

The Seller’s statements that these positions are “market”, “agreed” or “FINAL” have no contractual effect. They should be checked against any signed heads of agreement or documented principal-level decisions, but otherwise should not constrain the Buyer’s mark-up.

---

# 1. Liability regime

## General warranty cap

A 20% cap—AUD 4.8 million—leaves the Buyer carrying most of the downside if the acquired business is materially different from that warranted.

A 20% cap may be encountered for general business warranties, but the appropriate outcome depends on diligence, the quality of disclosure, insurance and the risk allocation elsewhere. It is not appropriate to extend that cap to title, tax, specific indemnities or known matters.

**Push back:**

- Seek a higher general warranty cap, particularly if there is no W&I insurance or escrow.
- Consider a meaningful holdback, escrow or W&I policy if Seller covenant strength is uncertain.
- Make clear that the cap does not apply to:
  - title, capacity, authority and capitalisation warranties;
  - tax covenant and tax warranties;
  - specific indemnities;
  - debt, leakage and purchase-price adjustments;
  - completion obligations and post-completion covenants;
  - fraud, fraudulent concealment, dishonesty or wilful misconduct;
  - claims that cannot lawfully be limited.

## De minimis and basket

The AUD 25,000 de minimis could exclude numerous recurring SaaS issues which are individually small but collectively significant. The AUD 250,000 basket is approximately 1.04% of price and is drafted as a **deductible**, meaning the Buyer permanently bears the first AUD 250,000.

**Push back:**

- Use a lower de minimis, or allow related claims and claims arising from a common cause to be aggregated.
- Make the basket a **tipping basket**: once exceeded, the entire valid amount is recoverable.
- Exclude title, tax, indemnity, leakage, debt and misconduct claims from both thresholds.
- Prevent the Seller from dividing one underlying problem into multiple sub-threshold claims.

## Time limits

Eighteen months may be insufficient to identify issues that emerge only after a full annual reporting, audit and customer-renewal cycle. Applying that period to “all Claims” is unacceptable.

**Push back:**

- General warranties: at least 24 months after Completion.
- Title, capacity, ownership and capitalisation: six years or the maximum period permitted by law.
- Tax: until expiry of the relevant statutory assessment period, plus an appropriate buffer and any extension where an audit or dispute is underway.
- Specific indemnities: a period tailored to the risk, or until finally resolved.
- Completion covenants, debt, leakage and price adjustments: their own express regimes.

A claim should be preserved by timely notice containing reasonable available details. It should not fail merely because the precise loss cannot yet be quantified. Contingent claims should remain alive once notified.

## Exclusive remedy and non-reliance

Applying limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance language to “all Claims of any nature” could restrict:

- specific indemnities;
- debt and price-adjustment rights;
- enforcement of completion obligations;
- restitution and equitable relief;
- misleading or deceptive conduct claims;
- fraud and deliberate concealment.

**Push back:** confine the warranty limitations to contractual warranty claims only. Expressly preserve the excluded categories above and injunctive, specific-performance and other equitable remedies. Nothing should purport to exclude liability that cannot legally be excluded.

---

# 2. Title and fundamental warranties

The share register is evidence of registered ownership, but it is not sufficient verification that the Buyer will receive 100% of the shares free of competing interests.

The Buyer also needs assurance regarding:

- beneficial ownership;
- absence of options, warrants, convertibles or other rights to securities;
- fully paid status;
- absence of security interests, trusts and third-party rights;
- valid issuance and transfers;
- Seller authority and capacity;
- completeness of the Company’s capital structure.

**Push back:**

- Title and fundamental warranties should be capped at **100% of the purchase price**, not 20%.
- They should have a substantially longer claim period.
- Require share certificates or an agreed lost-certificate process, executed transfers, updated registers, corporate approvals and relevant searches.
- Require all security interests affecting the shares or Company assets to be released at Completion.

---

# 3. Disclosure and buyer knowledge

## General data-room disclosure

Clauses 1.1 and 1.2 purport to disclose every fact contained or referred to anywhere in the data room, accounts, registers and public records. That is not adequate buyer protection. A matter may be technically present in a large data set without the nature, scope and consequences of the issue being apparent.

The disclosure cut-off is also **22 September 2026**, well before the current review date, creating a staleness and update risk.

**Push back:**

- Only matters **fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify their nature, scope and reasonably foreseeable consequences** should qualify warranties.
- Specific disclosure should be made against the relevant warranty.
- Public records and the accounts should not be generally deemed disclosed.
- If any data-room disclosure is accepted, it should be limited to a final, indexed, locked archive delivered with the executed SPA.
- Require an updated disclosure letter shortly before signing or Completion, but no new disclosure should qualify warranties without Buyer consent.
- Require warranties to be repeated at Completion, subject only to agreed disclosures.

Clause 1.4’s “no admission” reservation should not turn an incomplete factual description into effective disclosure. The Seller bears the burden of establishing that a matter was fairly disclosed.

## Buyer knowledge

The proposed provision excludes claims for matters known by the Buyer, its advisers, or discoverable in the data room or public records. That creates broad constructive and imputed knowledge and undermines the purpose of contractual warranties.

**Push back:**

- Prefer no buyer-knowledge exclusion.
- If one is unavoidable, limit it to the **actual, conscious knowledge** of a short list of named senior Buyer deal-team members at signing.
- Exclude deemed, constructive and imputed knowledge.
- Do not attribute advisers’ knowledge to the Buyer.
- The Seller should bear the burden of proving actual knowledge.
- Knowledge should not affect claims under specific indemnities, title warranties, tax covenants, fraud provisions or completion obligations.

---

# 4. Bluefen customer consent

Bluefen represents about AUD 3.6 million of FY26 revenue—approximately 30%. The consent is therefore a fundamental value and completion risk.

The Seller proposes merely to use reasonable endeavours and deem the condition satisfied upon delivery of a written consent. That is inadequate because:

- the consent may be conditional;
- clause 11.3 conditions may remain unsatisfied;
- Bluefen may require price reductions, concessions or contract amendments;
- the consent may reserve termination or other rights.

**Push back:**

Make Completion conditional on:

- receipt of final, unconditional and irrevocable written consent or waiver in agreed form;
- satisfaction or waiver of all clause 11.3 conditions;
- no adverse amendment, concession, fee, waiver or liability without Buyer consent;
- Bluefen confirming that the agreement remains in full force and it will not exercise termination or other adverse rights arising from the transaction.

The condition should be for the Buyer’s benefit, with Buyer discretion to waive it. The Seller should promptly provide all communications with Bluefen. If consent is not obtained by the long-stop date, the Buyer should be able to terminate without liability.

---

# 5. Riverlark facility and debt-free/cash-free completion

Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding and the Seller proposes to provide a release **after Completion**. That is directly inconsistent with debt-free/cash-free completion and exposes the Buyer to acquiring a company subject to debt and security.

**Push back:**

At or before Completion require:

- a current payout letter;
- payment of the facility from Seller sale proceeds or direct payment by the Buyer under an agreed funds flow;
- executed releases of all guarantees and security;
- documents sufficient to discharge PPSR registrations and any other registrations;
- release of any share security;
- confirmation that the facility cannot be redrawn;
- delivery of evidence of discharge promptly after filing.

Funds may be held in escrow pending filing mechanics, but the substantive release must be unconditional at Completion. Any outstanding principal, interest, break fee, discharge cost or other amount must be treated as debt and reduce the Seller’s proceeds dollar-for-dollar.

---

# 6. Purchase price, bonuses and other debt-like items

The AUD 420,000 Completion bonuses are triggered by the sale but are omitted from the completion funds flow. They are a Seller transaction cost, not an operating cost that should pass to the Buyer. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs may increase the amount.

**Push back:**

- Treat all bonuses and associated payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs as transaction expenses or debt-like items.
- Deduct them from the amount paid to the Seller, or require the Seller to fund them in full at Completion.
- Include a broad definition of transaction expenses capturing adviser costs, success fees, retention or change-of-control payments and related taxes.
- Require a complete employee-by-employee calculation and evidence of payment.

The AUD 180,000 Ironquay amount may also be a debt-like or transaction item if it must be paid to perfect ownership of assets included in the valuation.

The agreement needs a robust debt-free/cash-free mechanism—completion accounts or tightly drafted locked-box protections—with clear definitions of debt, cash, transaction expenses, leakage and working capital.

---

# 7. Ironquay intellectual property

Ownership of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on full payment, and AUD 180,000 remains open. For a SaaS target, uncertainty over ownership of development materials is potentially fundamental. Limiting the indemnity to the unpaid invoice does not cover the Buyer’s real exposure, including infringement claims, loss of ownership, replacement costs, business interruption or reduced value.

**Push back:**

Before Completion require:

- payment of all SOW3 fees by the Seller or as a deduction from Seller proceeds;
- a receipt and confirmation from Ironquay that all conditions to transfer have been satisfied;
- a confirmatory assignment of all relevant IP, source code, materials and associated rights;
- confirmation that Ironquay retains no lien, licence restriction or termination right affecting use.

The indemnity should cover all losses arising from:

- non-payment;
- failure of ownership or transfer;
- competing rights or liens;
- infringement arising from Ironquay deliverables;
- enforcement, remediation and replacement costs.

It should sit outside the general cap, basket and time limit, or have a bespoke cap reflecting the potential business impact.

---

# 8. Export/privacy incident

The disclosure does not establish whether the file was accessed, its exact contents, whether it involved personal information, or whether notification is required. The absence of a confirmed breach or quantified loss is not reassuring; it confirms that the investigation is incomplete.

Potential exposure includes regulatory notification, contractual breach, customer claims, remediation costs and reputational harm.

**Push back:**

Require before Completion:

- preservation and forensic review of access and download logs;
- confirmation of the precise data set, recipients and access status;
- containment and deletion evidence;
- assessment by privacy/cyber counsel of Privacy Act, Notifiable Data Breaches and contractual notification obligations;
- copies of relevant customer and regulator communications;
- details of cyber insurance notification and coverage;
- implementation of remediation measures.

Seek a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident and any pre-Completion related event, outside the general basket and cap. Require notification and remediation decisions before Completion to be made in consultation with the Buyer. Depending on the investigation outcome, completion should be conditional on satisfactory containment and absence of material regulatory or customer consequences.

---

# 9. Supplier renewals

The three Sandbar renewals total AUD 330,000. The disclosure deliberately does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. The Seller’s unsupported characterisation as ordinary-course cost should not determine treatment.

**Push back:**

Obtain the complete contracts, renewal notices and invoices and confirm:

- commencement and service periods;
- cancellation and termination rights;
- whether commitments were entered into before signing;
- whether amounts are accrued, overdue or prepaid;
- whether pricing or scope differs from past practice;
- whether the suppliers are related or the renewals are commercially linked.

Pre-Completion accrued amounts should be reflected in working capital or debt-like items as appropriate. Any non-ordinary-course commitment, early renewal or value-shifting arrangement should require Buyer consent and potentially a purchase-price adjustment or indemnity.

---

# 10. Office lease and Mossvale

The office lease appears to involve notification rather than consent, but the actual provision must be checked. Require timely compliance and evidence that no default, termination or fee results.

Mossvale’s assignment restriction may not apply to a share sale, but the full contract should be reviewed for:

- change-of-control language;
- deemed assignment provisions;
- termination rights;
- notification requirements;
- restrictions applying to indirect transfers.

These points should not be treated as resolved merely by the Seller’s characterisation.

---

# Recommended negotiation position

## Signing/completion blockers

1. **Bluefen:** unconditional consent and satisfaction of all conditions.
2. **Riverlark:** full repayment and effective release at Completion.
3. **Ironquay:** payment and confirmed IP transfer.
4. **Privacy incident:** completed investigation, containment and acceptable remediation.
5. **Funds flow:** deduction or Seller funding of bonuses, on-costs, debt and transaction expenses.

## Liability protections

6. Reject applying the 20%/18-month regime to all claims.
7. Title and fundamental warranties: 100% cap and long limitation period.
8. Separate tax protection and bespoke indemnities for Ironquay, the privacy incident and other identified liabilities.
9. Carve out debt, leakage, price adjustments, covenants, misconduct and non-excludable statutory rights.
10. Seek a tipping basket, lower thresholds and aggregation of related claims.

## Disclosure protections

11. Reject blanket data-room and public-register disclosure.
12. Require fair, specific disclosure with sufficient detail.
13. Limit buyer knowledge to actual knowledge of named individuals, if accepted at all.
14. Require a locked disclosure archive, updated diligence and warranties repeated at Completion.
15. Do not allow unilateral supplemental disclosure to qualify warranties after signing.

Overall, Wattlebridge should not accept the package as an integrated “balanced” bargain. Several matters presented as disclosures are actually **unresolved completion risks or quantified Seller liabilities** and should be cleared, priced or specifically indemnified—not merely disclosed.

- payment of all SOW3 fees by the Seller or as a deduction from Seller proceeds;
- a receipt and confirmation from Ironquay that all conditions to transfer have been satisfied;
- a confirmatory assignment of all relevant IP, source code, materials and associated rights;
- confirmation that Ironquay retains no lien, licence restriction or termination right affecting use.

The indemnity should cover all losses arising from:

- non-payment;
- failure of ownership or transfer;
- competing rights or liens;
- infringement arising from Ironquay deliverables;
- enforcement, remediation and replacement costs.

It should sit outside the general cap, basket and time limit, or have a bespoke cap reflecting the potential business impact.

---

# 8. Export/privacy incident

The disclosure does not establish whether the file was accessed, its exact contents, whether it involved personal information, or whether notification is required. The absence of a confirmed breach or quantified loss is not reassuring; it confirms that the investigation is incomplete.

Potential exposure includes regulatory notification, contractual breach, customer claims, remediation costs and reputational harm.

**Push back:**

Require before Completion:

- preservation and forensic review of access and download logs;
- confirmation of the precise data set, recipients and access status;
- containment and deletion evidence;
- assessment by privacy/cyber counsel of Privacy Act, Notifiable Data Breaches and contractual notification obligations;
- copies of relevant customer and regulator communications;
- details of cyber insurance notification and coverage;
- implementation of remediation measures.

Seek a specific indemnity for all losses arising from the incident and any pre-Completion related event, outside the general basket and cap. Require notification and remediation decisions before Completion to be made in consultation with the Buyer. Depending on the investigation outcome, completion should be conditional on satisfactory containment and absence of material regulatory or customer consequences.

---

# 9. Supplier renewals

The three Sandbar renewals total AUD 330,000. The disclosure deliberately does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. The Seller’s unsupported characterisation as ordinary-course cost should not determine treatment.

**Push back:**

Obtain the complete contracts, renewal notices and invoices and confirm:

- commencement and service periods;
- cancellation and termination rights;
- whether commitments were entered into before signing;
- whether amounts are accrued, overdue or prepaid;
- whether pricing or scope differs from past practice;
- whether the suppliers are related or the renewals are commercially linked.

Pre-Completion accrued amounts should be reflected in working capital or debt-like items as appropriate. Any non-ordinary-course commitment, early renewal or value-shifting arrangement should require Buyer consent and potentially a purchase-price adjustment or indemnity.

---

# 10. Office lease and Mossvale

The office lease appears to involve notification rather than consent, but the actual provision must be checked. Require timely compliance and evidence that no default, termination or fee results.

Mossvale’s assignment restriction may not apply to a share sale, but the full contract should be reviewed for:

- change-of-control language;
- deemed assignment provisions;
- termination rights;
- notification requirements;
- restrictions applying to indirect transfers.

These points should not be treated as resolved merely by the Seller’s characterisation.

# Recommended negotiation position

## Signing/completion blockers

1. **Bluefen:** unconditional consent and satisfaction of all conditions.
2. **Riverlark:** full repayment and effective release at Completion.
3. **Ironquay:** payment and confirmed IP transfer.
4. **Privacy incident:** completed investigation, containment and acceptable remediation.
5. **Funds flow:** deduction or Seller funding of bonuses, on-costs, debt and transaction expenses.

## Liability protections

6. Reject applying the 20%/18-month regime to all claims.
7. Title and fundamental warranties: 100% cap and long limitation period.
8. Separate tax protection and bespoke indemnities for Ironquay, the privacy incident and other identified liabilities.
9. Carve out debt, leakage, price adjustments, covenants, misconduct and non-excludable statutory rights.
10. Seek a tipping basket, lower thresholds and aggregation of related claims.

## Disclosure protections

11. Reject blanket data-room and public-register disclosure.
12. Require fair, specific disclosure with sufficient detail.
13. Limit buyer knowledge to actual knowledge of named individuals, if accepted at all.
14. Require a locked disclosure archive, updated diligence and warranties repeated at Completion.
15. Do not allow unilateral supplemental disclosure to qualify warranties after signing.

Overall, Wattlebridge should not accept the package as an integrated “balanced” bargain. Several matters presented as disclosures are actually **unresolved completion risks or quantified Seller liabilities** and should be cleared, priced or specifically indemnified—not merely disclosed.
